source.title: Towards Understanding the Nature of Attention with Low-Rank Sparse Decomposition
source.authors: Zheng-Fu He; Junxuan Wang; Rui Lin; Xu-Yang Ge; Wentao Shu; Qiong Tang; Junping Zhang; Xi-Peng Qiu

record.tranche_reason: The study identifies induction-like attention units and uses path patching and attribution to examine their contributions, but it does not reproduce the original training-time measurements of induction-head emergence and in-context learning.
record.gate_note: The study reports induction-head interpretations in Pythia-160M Lorsa and path-patching scores for MHSA heads’ contributions to induction behavior. It also reports an induction attribution graph for a 2-layer Transformer. Statements about induction heads cited from prior work are not treated as results here. The study does not report induction-head emergence over training, a loss bump, or in-context learning loss-by-token measurements.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper on Lorsa, a sparse replacement for attention. Induction heads serve as a known mechanism to validate that Lorsa rediscovers prior head types. The paper does not test whether induction heads form by composing with a previous-token head in small attention-only models (V1). It does not test training dynamics (V2, V7), in-context-learning share (V3, V6), data dependence (V5), or systematic cross-model universality (V4). The Pythia-160M path-patching table (Table 6) does locate induction heads in one model. That restates well-documented heads, is used to cross-reference Lorsa heads, and defines no induction metric or baseline. The 2-layer induction circuit is shown only as a figure, with no numbers. The authors also state they failed to find Lorsa heads with Q/K composition.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that Lorsa recovers known attention mechanisms (induction, name mover, successor and copy-suppression heads, and attention sinks) as finer-grained units, and finds new ones such as arithmetic heads. They state their early attempts to find Lorsa heads with Q/K composition failed, and list systematic Q/K/V composition as future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a sparse replacement for pretrained MHSA to interpret attention units, then uses head interpretation, path patching, and attribution. It does not reproduce the original training-time induction-head and in-context-learning measurements.

fits_no_version.finding: A Lorsa induction unit is spread across two MHSA heads (5.0 and 5.7). Lorsa finds token-specific induction units (e.g. for 'you', last names, abbreviations), so induction behaviour is split into finer units than whole heads.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Induction behaviour in pretrained LMs decomposes into many token- or domain-specific sparse attention units, some superposed across several heads.

fits_no_version.finding: Path patching in Pythia-160M concentrates induction contribution in L5.0 (4.00), with smaller contributions from L4.6, L5.7, L9.0 and L5.6. Several heads show large negative values (e.g. L3.3 -1.20, L9.4 -1.10).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Induction behaviour in Pythia-160M is concentrated in one dominant layer-5 head, with other heads opposing it.

record.problems: The induction-head findings are interpretive case studies, not a systematic measurement across models or training runs. The authors report that they failed in early attempts to find Lorsa heads with QK composition. The 2-layer model is explicitly described as capability-constrained.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix F.3, Table 6 reports path-patching values for every MHSA head. Only the five heads explicitly highlighted by the authors are included; the remaining per-head cells are omitted as non-highlighted entries in a table exceeding the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Composition of an induction head with an earlier previous-token head in small attention-only models. The authors report failing to find Lorsa heads with Q/K composition. The 2-layer circuit (Fig. 15) has no quantitative description.
All of it; there is no training-time data.
Only one model (Pythia-160M) has an induction-head search, so there is no cross-family or cross-run comparison.

record.verdict_notes: Induction heads serve here as a validation target for a new interpretability method. R10's head ID appears mismatched with Table 2. Negative path-patching cells in Table 6 were omitted from the rows; they are noted under fits_no_version. The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The study identifies induction behavior and provides an attribution graph for induction behavior, but does not report a detailed test that an earlier previous-token head composes with a later head to implement the full mechanism.
Training-time onset, abruptness, in-context-learning gain, and training-loss bump.
Whether induction heads carry most in-context learning in large transformers.
Induction behavior is not systematically tested across model families, sizes, training runs, architectures, or modalities.
No comparison of data or training setups for their effects on induction-head formation or persistent in-context learning.
No comparison of few-shot task learning mechanisms against token-copying behavior.
No test of whether induction-head formation comprises multiple transitions.
